sermon:
## The Vapor and the Grave
*What a closed world can never give you*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 1:1-18 · **Supporting:** Genesis 3:19; Psalm 90:10; Romans 8:20; 1 Corinthians 15:17

There is a kind of honesty most preachers will not risk. The Preacher of Ecclesiastes risks it in his first breath. He does not open with comfort. He opens with a verdict that should empty the room, and instead it has held readers for three thousand years, because every one of us has felt it on some gray afternoon when the work was done and the silence came in and nothing in the house had anything left to say to us.

**The word he keeps saying**
The Hebrew is *hevel*. We translate it "vanity," but the word means vapor, breath, mist, the cloud you can see and cannot hold. "Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities. All is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). He is not saying life is worthless. He is saying life is a vapor, here, then gone, slipping through the fingers of the man who grips hardest. Then he asks the question the whole book turns on: "What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?" (1:3). Gain. Profit. What is left in your hand at the close of the ledger. And the answer, under the sun, is nothing. The sun comes up and goes down and hurries back to rise again. The rivers run to the sea and the sea is never full. The eye is never satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. "All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it" (1:8). The wheel turns and turns and arrives nowhere, and the generations come and go, and the earth forgets them. "There is no remembrance of former things" (1:11). Your name, the thing you spent a life making unforgettable, will be forgotten. Walk through any old cemetery and read the stones until the names mean nothing, because the people who knew those names are themselves under stones a little further down the hill. "What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun" (1:9). The Preacher is not being cynical. He is being exact.

Three words decide everything in this book: *under the sun*. The Preacher is conducting an experiment. He shuts the ceiling. He reasons as though there were nothing above the sun, no throne, no judgment, no resurrection, and he asks what life adds up to inside that sealed room. This is not unbelief. It is the most rigorous believer in Scripture showing you exactly what your life equals if God is not real. He grants the skeptic his premise and follows it all the way down, further than the skeptic himself is usually willing to go.

**Why the wisdom does not save him**
The Preacher is not a simple man who never read. "I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven" (1:13). He is the one who knew the most. And his learning did not lift him out of the vapor, it pressed him deeper into it. "For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (1:18). This is the part the modern world cannot answer. We were told that if we just knew more, mapped more, measured more, the ache would lift. The Preacher knew more than anyone alive, and knowing more only let him see the futility in higher resolution. The smarter you are, the more clearly you see the wheel, and the wheel does not stop turning because you understood it.

Genesis already told us why. The man was made of dust, and to the dust he was sentenced to return: "you are dust, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:19). Paul names the same wound at the root of the world, "the creation was subjected to futility" (Romans 8:20). That word, futility, is the Greek translators reaching for the Preacher's *hevel*. The vapor is not a mood. It is the curse running under the floorboards of a fallen world. Moses counted the years and got seventy, eighty if the strength holds, "yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away" (Psalm 90:10). The grave erases the gain. That is the Preacher's whole case, and it is true.

**The honesty before the hope**
I have stood at gravesides and watched a family carry out a casket holding everything a man spent forty years building, and I have felt the Preacher's verdict settle over the room like dust. And I will tell you what I have done with that feeling more times than I want to admit, I have rushed it. I have reached for the bright closing word before the people in front of me had finished feeling the weight. I wanted to relieve the pressure the text creates, because the pressure is hard to stand inside, even for the man holding the Bible. The Preacher will not let me. He makes me sit in the room with the closed ceiling, because a hope offered before the diagnosis is honest is not hope. It is sedation.

Here is what the closed ceiling cannot account for. An empty tomb. The whole book reasons under the sun, and the answer to the book is something that happened over it, a Friday grave that did not hold. Paul put the stakes exactly where the Preacher put them: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile" (1 Corinthians 15:17). Futile. *Hevel*. Vapor. Paul agrees with the Preacher completely. If the grave is the end, then the Preacher is right and we are fools to argue with him. But the grave was not the end. Christ broke the ceiling open, and the gain the Preacher could not find under the sun was buried with a body that walked out of its own tomb three days later. The vapor was real. It was never the last word.

Everything under the sun passes.

## You Cannot Keep What You Build
*The wise man and the fool share one grave*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 2:1-26 · **Supporting:** Luke 12:20; Psalm 49:10; Matthew 6:19-20; 1 Timothy 6:7

Most of us never run the experiment because we cannot afford it. The Preacher could. He had the throne, the treasury, the unlimited budget, and he spent it all on a single question, will more finally be enough? He is the one man in history who got to test the dream the rest of us only finance on credit. And he came back from it to tell us what is on the other side of getting everything.

**The man who tried it all**
Read what he built. "I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees... I had also great possessions of herds and flocks... I gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces" (Ecclesiastes 2:4-8). Count the phrase he keeps repeating, *for myself*. It runs through the passage like a refrain. This is the most self-directed life ever lived, and he held nothing back: "whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure" (2:10). Pleasure, wine, work, music, folly, wisdom, he ran the whole menu. He was not a bored prince dabbling. He was a serious man conducting a serious test, and he kept his wisdom through all of it so that he could stand back and observe the results with a clear head. "And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil" (2:10). For a while it worked. The pleasure was real. The work was satisfying in the doing of it. The Preacher does not deny that there was joy in the building. He denies that the joy lasted, or that anything was left of it once the man who built it was gone.

Then the morning after. "Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had spent in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun" (2:11). He turned around to look at the empire he had built and saw vapor. Not because the gardens were ugly. They were magnificent. But magnificence does not change the arithmetic the Preacher cannot escape, and he was too honest to pretend it did.

**The leveling fact**
Here is the fact that ruined it for him. "The wise dies just like the fool" (2:16). He had spent his life becoming wiser than every man before him, and the grave does not check your credentials at the door. "How the wise dies just like the fool. So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me" (2:16-17). The Psalmist had already seen it: "For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others" (Psalm 49:10). One grave for the genius and the idiot. One ending for the builder and the man who never lifted a hammer in his life. The grave is the great leveler, and it does not negotiate rates for the accomplished.

And then the second blow, sharper than the first. He has to leave it all to a man he did not choose and cannot vet. "I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled" (2:18-19). You break your body for forty years, and the whole pile passes in an afternoon to an heir who might burn it down by Thursday. "This also is vanity and a great evil" (2:21). Paul said it plainly to Timothy, "we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world" (1 Timothy 6:7). The hands that built it close empty in the casket. Every hearse pulls an empty trailer. The Preacher had watched men spend their whole strength assembling something they were certain would outlast them, and he had watched that something dispersed within a generation by people who never knew the cost of it. He is not bitter about this. He is simply unwilling to lie to you about it the way the rest of the world will.

**The idol I keep rebuilding**
I know this idol because I have served it. Not with palaces, with the quieter version, the one that hides better in a pastor. I have measured a year by what I produced. I have looked back at the work of my hands and asked it to tell me I mattered, and the work cannot answer, and I keep asking anyway. The Preacher is not describing a king from long ago. He is describing the thing every one of us does when we build a self out of what we can accumulate and then beg the pile to justify our existence. It never does. It cannot. The pile is going to someone else, and the someone else may not even keep it.

This is the man Jesus drew with one sentence. The barns are full, the soul is satisfied, the plan is set, and God speaks: "Fool. This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" (Luke 12:20). Whose will they be. The Preacher's exact terror, on the lips of Christ. And Jesus does not leave us in the barn. He points us to the only treasure that survives the night: "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matthew 6:19-20). The Preacher could not find a gain the grave would not take. Christ went into the grave and came back holding one, and he holds it out to people whose barns are already failing.

You cannot keep what you build.

## You Are Not the Timekeeper
*Eternity in the heart, the work hidden from the eye*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 3:1-22 · **Supporting:** Psalm 31:15; Acts 1:7; Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 11:33

We have turned the most famous lines in Ecclesiastes into something soothing. We read "a time for everything" on funeral cards and gentle plaques, and we miss what the Preacher is actually doing. He is not comforting you. He is telling you who runs the clock, and it is not you.

**The seasons you did not set**
"For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die... a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance... a time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Ecclesiastes 3:1-7). Read it again and notice, you appointed none of these. You did not pick the day you were born. You will not pick the day you die. You did not schedule the season of mourning that fell on your house, and you cannot order the season of dancing to come back on command. The seasons come on their own authority, and the whole list is a quiet argument that there is a hand on the clock and the hand is not yours. The Preacher is not handing you a poem about balance. He is taking the timepiece out of your fingers, one line at a time.

Then he says the thing that goes deeper than anything else in the book. "He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end" (3:11). Eternity in the heart. That is why the vapor grieves you. An animal does not stand at a grave and ache for forever, it has no eternity planted in it. You do. You were built for a country you have never seen, given a homesickness for a place you cannot name, and then set down inside a span of seventy years that cannot satisfy the longing. That ache you have felt at the edge of a beautiful evening, the one that turns to grief for no reason you can explain, the one that comes precisely when things are good and you cannot understand why your chest hurts, that is not a defect. It is the fingerprint of God on a creature made for more than the sun. The beauty was a gift and it pointed past itself, and the ache is your heart recognizing that the gift is not the home.

**The book you cannot read**
And here is the limit he sets, hard. God has made everything beautiful in its time, "yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end" (3:11). You have eternity in your chest and a closed book in your hands. You can feel that the story means something. You cannot read the whole of it. You get your one chapter, and the plot of the chapters before and after is sealed against you.

This is the wall every one of us hits in the dark. Why this loss, why now, why in this order, why the good man and not the cruel one. Moses drew the same line: "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children" (Deuteronomy 29:29). There is a revealed world you are responsible for, and a secret world that is none of your business, and most of our anguish comes from pounding on the door of the second one. Paul stood at the same wall and did not break it down, he bowed. "Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God. How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways" (Romans 11:33). The Preacher's posture and Paul's are the same. Reverence in front of a door you cannot open.

**The hand I keep trying to grab**
I will tell you what I do, because I suspect you do it too. I try to take the clock back. I lie awake auditing God's timing, certain that if I had been holding the schedule I would have arranged the losses more reasonably, spaced the griefs further apart, opened the doors I am still standing in front of and closed the ones I wanted closed. I have prayed, in everything but these words, "give me the timekeeping back, because I would do it better than you have." That is a fearful thing to confess from a pulpit, and it is true. Every time, the Preacher and the cross take my hand off the clock and put it somewhere else.

David found the only place for that hand to rest. "My times are in your hand" (Psalm 31:15). Not in mine. In his. And when the disciples stood with the risen Christ and demanded the schedule, is it now, is this the season, Jesus refused them the clock too: "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority" (Acts 1:7). The same word the Preacher used. Times and seasons. Fixed by the Father, withheld from us, and we can bear the withholding now, because the One who holds the times went to a cross at the right time, on a Friday he did not avoid, for people who could not save themselves. Paul wrote that "at the right time Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6). The right time. Not the time the disciples would have picked, not the time that made sense to anyone watching it happen, but the time appointed by the hand that holds all the times. The hand on the clock has nail marks in it. You can trust a hand like that with the hours you cannot see, and with the ones that have already wounded you.

You are not the timekeeper.

## No Man Should Toil Alone
*Oppression without a comforter, and the small mercy of two*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 4:1-16 · **Supporting:** Genesis 2:18; Galatians 6:2; John 16:33; Hebrews 10:24-25

The Preacher has been looking at the world from a throne. In chapter four he gets up and walks down into the street, and what he sees there is the loneliness of people grinding through their lives with no one beside them. This is the most pastoral chapter in the book, and it begins with tears.

**The oppressed with no one to comfort them**
"Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them. On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them" (Ecclesiastes 4:1). He says it twice in one verse, no one to comfort them, no one to comfort them. The repetition is the wound. The Preacher is not most disturbed by the oppression itself, terrible as it is. He is disturbed by the aloneness inside it, the crushing that happens with no hand on the shoulder, no second person in the room when the weight comes down. The cruelest part of suffering is often that you carry it by yourself.

Then he diagnoses the engine running underneath all our striving, and it is not need. It is envy. "Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind" (4:4). We are not working to live. We are working to beat the man next to us, and we have dressed the rivalry up as ambition and called it healthy. And it isolates us, because you cannot be a brother to the man you are racing. The Preacher then draws the loneliest figure in the book, the man with no one, no son, no brother, who never stops working: "yet his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, 'For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?'" (4:8). For whom. He has forgotten to ask the only question that would have saved him. He is heaping up a fortune for an empty house, and he will die in that house alone.

**The mercy of two**
And here the Preacher gives one of the few warm gifts in the whole book. "Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up" (4:9-10). It is not a grand solution to the vapor. It is a small, sturdy mercy. The man who falls and has someone to lift him is not exempt from the futility, he still falls. He simply does not fall alone. "And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him. A threefold cord is not quickly broken" (4:12). The Preacher knows life will knock you down. He is telling you not to be standing by yourself when it does.

This was the first thing in all creation God called not good. Everything in Genesis was good, good, good, and then one verdict broke the pattern: "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). Before the fall, before any sin, in a perfect garden with unbroken fellowship with God himself, the man needed another human being. Solitude was the first thing heaven named a problem. The Preacher under the sun arrives at exactly what God said in the garden. We were not built to toil alone, and the world that tells you to be self-sufficient is selling you the loneliest lie there is.

**What I built my isolation out of**
I have to tell you what I have done with this, because the loneliest man in this chapter is often the one standing in the pulpit. I have hidden the falls. I have decided it was strength to carry the weight where no one could see it, and I have called that strength when it was only pride wearing a collar. I have let people lift each other in my church while quietly arranging my own life so that no one would ever have to lift me, because being the one who is lifted felt like weakness, and weakness felt like the end of my usefulness. The Preacher names that man. He is not strong. He is the man with no one to comfort him, and he built the aloneness himself, brick by careful brick.

Paul refused to let the church live that way. "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). The whole law of Christ, fulfilled in two people carrying one weight. And the writer of Hebrews tells us not to drift into the lonely life, "not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another" (Hebrews 10:25). This is why the church exists in bodies and not just in our heads. But the deepest comfort is not that we have each other. It is that the man of sorrows refused to stay above our aloneness, he came down into the oppression and the tears and the falling, and he said, "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). The Preacher saw oppressed people with no one to comfort them, weeping with no hand on their shoulder. Then God himself walked into the street, into the oppression and the tears, and became the comforter who would not leave, and who sends his people to be the hands that lift each other up when one of them falls. The threefold cord the Preacher commended is, in the end, Christ binding two fallen people together and refusing to let either of them break.

No man should toil alone.

## Fear God and Keep Your Vows
*Few words above, kept promises below*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 5:1-20 · **Supporting:** Matthew 6:7; James 5:12; 1 Timothy 6:10; Philippians 4:11

We come to church having decided in advance that we are the ones with something to offer. We bring our words, our requests, our running commentary on God, and the Preacher stops us at the door with a sentence that should reorder how every one of us prays. He tells us to watch our feet.

**Guard your steps**
"Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil" (Ecclesiastes 5:1). Draw near to listen. Not to perform, not to inform God of your opinions, to listen. And then the line that should silence half of what passes for worship: "Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few" (5:2). God is in heaven and you are on earth. The Preacher locates you. He is not crushing you; he is orienting you. There is a distance between the Creator and the creature, and the right response to that distance is not chatter. It is reverence, and reverence speaks carefully.

This is precisely what Jesus taught when he warned against the prayers that try to wear God down with volume. "And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words" (Matthew 6:7). The Preacher and the Lord agree completely. The God of heaven is not impressed by the length of your speech. He is honored by the seriousness of your few words. A man who truly knew who was on the other side of the prayer would not be careless with it.

**The vow you said and forgot**
Then the Preacher turns to the thing we said to God in a hard moment and never thought about again. "When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay" (5:4-5). We make our promises in the foxhole, if you get me through this, I will change, I will give, I will follow, and the moment the danger passes, the vow evaporates with it. The Preacher says God remembers what you said even when you have forgotten it. "Let not your mouth lead you into sin" (5:6). James drew the same line tight: "let your 'yes' be yes and your 'no' be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation" (James 5:12). A people who fear God are a people whose word holds after the crisis passes.

And then he turns to the appetite that never closes, money. "He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income. This also is vanity" (5:10). The love of money is a thirst that drinking only deepens. Paul named it the root: "For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith" (1 Timothy 6:10). But the Preacher does not leave us in despair over our possessions. He hands us the secret the rich man could never find: "Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun... this is his lot... this is the gift of God" (5:18-19). The gift of God. Enjoyment is not something you seize. It is something you receive, your bread and your work taken from God's hand as a portion, not hoarded as a hedge against a future you cannot control anyway.

**The prayers I have heaped up**
I know the sacrifice of fools because I have offered it. I have come into God's presence rash with my mouth, full of my agenda, treating the throne of heaven like a counter where I place my orders and check my watch. I have made vows in the dark of a long night and let them dissolve by breakfast. And I have loved money in the disguise pastors are permitted, calling it security, calling it stewardship, while my heart did the same arithmetic as every anxious man, certain that a little more would finally still the fear. It never did. It never does. The Preacher told me it would not, and I did not believe him for years.

Paul learned the only cure, and he learned it in a prison cell, not a palace: "I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content" (Philippians 4:11). Contentment is not getting enough. It is receiving your portion from the hand of God and trusting that the hand is good. And we can trust that hand because of what it gave when we could give nothing back, the Son, the unrepayable gift, spent on people who had nothing to bring to the house of God but our need and our few honest words. That is why we draw near to listen. We are not there to inform heaven of anything heaven does not already know. We are there because heaven has already spoken its few, final words over us in a cross, and a man who has heard those words does not come into the house of God rash with his mouth. He comes in quiet, and he keeps what he promised, and he holds his money loosely, because he has already received the one gift that money could never buy and the grave can never take.

Fear God. Keep your vows.

## Having Is Not the Same as Enjoying
*The gift that comes without the power to taste it*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 6:1-12 · **Supporting:** Luke 12:15; Psalm 39:6; 1 Timothy 6:6-7; John 6:35

There is a grief so specific that most preaching steps around it, and the Preacher walks straight into the middle of it. It is the grief of the man who has everything and cannot enjoy any of it. We assume that the having is the problem solved. The Preacher tells us the having can be its own curse.

**The riches a man cannot taste**
"There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them" (Ecclesiastes 6:1-2). Read that carefully. God gives the wealth. God gives the honor. And God withholds the one thing that would make them mean anything, the power to enjoy them. The man has the full table and no hunger, the full house and no rest, and a stranger walks in and consumes what he could not. "This is vanity; it is a grievous evil" (6:2).

The Preacher is making a distinction we spend our whole lives refusing to make. Possession is one thing. Enjoyment is another, and the second is a gift that cannot be purchased with the first. You can buy the meal and not the appetite. You can buy the bed and not the sleep. You can buy the vacation and stand on the beach with your mind back in the office, unable to be where your body is. You can assemble the life everyone envies and stand inside it numb, and the Preacher says this is one of the heaviest evils under the sun, not that you lack, but that you have and cannot feel it.

**The appetite that is never filled**
Then he names the hunger that no amount can satisfy. "All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not filled" (6:7). The mouth keeps eating and the appetite keeps opening. He says a man could father a hundred children and live a thousand years twice over, and if his soul is not satisfied with good, a stillborn child is better off than he is (6:3-6). That is a hard saying, and he means it to be. Quantity is not the answer to a soul-shaped emptiness. More years, more children, more wealth, pour them all into a hole with no bottom and the hole is exactly as empty as before. The math of more never closes the gap, because the gap was never a math problem. We keep treating a spiritual emptiness as though it were a supply shortage, certain that the next acquisition is the one that finally lands. It is not, and the Preacher had more than any of us will ever have, and it did not land for him either.

Jesus said it in one sentence that should be carved over every shopping cart in the world: "Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions" (Luke 12:15). Does not consist. Your life is not the sum of what you own, and the man who stakes his life on that sum will starve at a full table. David saw the futility of the heaping itself: "Surely a man goes about as a shadow. Surely for nothing they are in turmoil; man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather" (Psalm 39:6). The Preacher closes the chapter with the wall again, "who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life... For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?" (6:12). No one knows what comes next. No one can read past the grave from this side of it.

**The hunger I keep feeding wrong**
I have an appetite I have spent years feeding the wrong food, and I suspect you do too. Mine is not for money, exactly, it is for the next accomplishment, the next sense that I have done enough, the next quiet evening when the striving will finally feel finished and I can rest. And every time I reach it, the appetite opens again the next morning, unfilled, asking for more, and I keep handing it the same food that has never once satisfied it. The Preacher is describing my soul with surgical precision. The hunger is real. It is not the problem. I have just been feeding it at the wrong table my whole life, and calling the emptiness a reason to work harder.

Paul found the only thing that fills it: "But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world" (1 Timothy 6:6-7). Great gain, the very word the Preacher hunted for under the sun and never found. And Jesus stood up in front of a hungry crowd and claimed to be the food the appetite was made for: "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst" (John 6:35). The Preacher diagnosed a hunger that nothing under the sun could fill. Then the bread came down from above the sun and offered himself to the starving. The man with everything could not enjoy it, because his soul was the wrong shape for everything the world could hand him. The man who has Christ can enjoy his bread and his work as a gift, because his soul is finally fed by the only thing that was ever the right size for it. And then, fed, he can sit down at an ordinary table on an ordinary evening and taste it, actually taste it, which is the gift the rich man in this chapter would have traded all his wealth to receive and never could.

Having is not the same as enjoying.

## Wisdom Knows What It Cannot Know
*The house of mourning teaches what the house of feasting cannot*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 7:1-29 · **Supporting:** Psalm 90:12; Job 28:28; Romans 7:24; Proverbs 9:10

We spend a fortune arranging our lives so that we never have to sit in a room with grief. The Preacher tells us that the room we are avoiding is the one classroom where the most important lesson is taught, and the party we are chasing teaches us nothing at all.

**The house of mourning**
"It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart" (Ecclesiastes 7:2). This offends everything in us. Better the funeral than the feast. Why? Because "sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The house of mourning does not lie to you. It tells you the truth the feast spends all night hiding, that you are going to die, that this is the end of all mankind, and that a life lived as though that were not true is a life lived as a fool. "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth" (7:4). The fool runs from the funeral. The wise man lets the funeral teach him what no celebration ever could. "It is better for a man to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools" (7:5). The song is sweeter going down. The rebuke is what changes you.

This is the great gift of remembered death. Moses prayed for it: "So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12). Wisdom is not the accumulation of facts. It begins with the honest count of how few your days are. The man who never visits the house of mourning never numbers his days, and the man who never numbers his days will waste every one of them on things that will not matter in the room where the casket is. The funeral is the teacher. The party is the distraction that costs you the lesson.

**The limit wisdom finds**
But here is the turn that keeps this chapter from becoming a lecture on being clever. The Preacher, the wisest man in the book, marks the place where wisdom hits its own ceiling. "Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked?" (7:13). You cannot. Some things are crooked by God's appointment, and no amount of wisdom will straighten them. He says he resolved to be wise, "but it was far from me. That which has been is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out?" (7:23-24). The wisest man alive reaches the edge of what wisdom can reach and tells you plainly that he cannot get to the bottom of God's scheme. Deep, very deep, and beyond him, and beyond you.

This is the whole book of Job, compressed. After all the speeches, all the friends, all the demands for an explanation, the verdict on wisdom comes down to one line: "And he said to man, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding'" (Job 28:28). Not mastery. Fear. The wise person is not the one who has God figured out, that person is a fool who has not yet noticed the depth of the water he is standing in. The wise person is the one who knows where the knowing stops and bows there. And the Preacher refuses both ditches, do not be overly righteous, do not be overly wicked, "for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them" (7:18). Wisdom that fears God walks the narrow road between self-righteous certainty and reckless folly, and it walks it humbly.

**The thing I cannot fix in myself**
I will name the crooked thing I keep trying to straighten, because it is the one in the mirror. It is me. I have spent years believing that with enough discipline, enough study, enough self-examination, I could finally straighten the bent thing in my own heart, the pride that wears the costume of humility, the fear I have named discernment, the contempt I have called conviction. And I cannot. The wisest man who ever lived reached the same wall: "See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes" (7:29). I am the crooked thing wisdom cannot straighten, and every honest hour of my life has told me so, and I have spent the next morning trying again with a new technique.

Paul reached that exact wall and finally stopped trying to climb it himself. "Wretched man that I am. Who will deliver me from this body of death?" (Romans 7:24). He does not answer the question with a method. He answers it with a person, thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. The crooked thing in you cannot be straightened by you. It was straightened on a cross by a wisdom from above the sun, a wisdom that did not explain the deep scheme of God so much as enter it and bear it. "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight" (Proverbs 9:10), and the cross is where the fear of God and the love of God meet, and where the crooked are finally made straight by the only one who could do it. The wisest man in the Old Testament took us to the edge of what wisdom can reach and stopped, honest, at the wall. The wisdom of God walked past that wall, into the deep scheme no one could find out, and came back with the crooked thing in us made straight. That is the only wisdom that saves, and it does not start with how much you know. It starts on your knees.

Wisdom knows what it cannot know.

## Remember Him Before the Dark
*Sow in the morning, rejoice with sober joy, before the body fails*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 11:1-12:8 · **Supporting:** John 9:4; Psalm 90:12; 2 Corinthians 9:6; James 4:14

The Preacher has spent the whole book telling us that everything passes. Now, near the end, he turns to the young and does the most surprising thing in the book. He does not tell them to despair. He tells them to live, and to live now, while the light holds, because the dark is coming and it does not negotiate.

**Sow while you can**
"Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days. Give a portion to seven, or even to eight, for you know not what disaster may happen on earth" (Ecclesiastes 11:1-2). This is the Preacher's answer to a future no one can read. Not paralysis, generosity. You do not know what is coming, so sow widely, give freely, scatter your bread on waters you cannot control. "He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap" (11:4). The man who waits for perfect conditions never plants anything. The future is uncertain, and the Preacher's response to uncertainty is not to hoard against it but to sow into it with open hands. Paul carried the same farming logic into the church: "Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully" (2 Corinthians 9:6).

And then he tells the young to be glad, but with a hook in the gladness. "Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment" (11:9). This is not the world's permission to do whatever you want. It is sober joy, real enjoyment of the days God gives, lived under the open eye of a God who will weigh it all. "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity" (11:10). Enjoy the light. Remember it is being watched, and remember it does not last.

**Before the body fails**
Then comes the most tender passage in the book, and the most urgent. "Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, 'I have no pleasure in them'" (12:1). And he paints old age in images no one forgets, the keepers of the house tremble, the strong men are bent, the grinders cease because they are few, those who look through the windows are dimmed, the doors on the street are shut (12:3-4). It is the body breaking down, room by room, the house of a man falling quiet, until "the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it" (12:7). The window for remembering does not stay open. The Preacher is not threatening the young. He is loving them enough to tell them the truth they least want to hear, there is a clock on this, and it is running, and the remembering gets harder, not easier, as the light goes.

Jesus felt this same urgency about his own working hours: "We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work" (John 9:4). While it is day. The day does not last. James said our lives are exactly the Preacher's word, vapor: "What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes" (James 4:14). The vapor that opened the book reappears at its end, and the only sane response to a vanishing life is to remember the One who gave it before it is gone.

**The thing I keep postponing**
I know the sin this passage names, because it is not the young man's sin only. It is mine, and it wears the disguise of responsibility. I tell myself I will give more freely later, when the margin is wider. I will rest in God more fully later, when the demands thin out. I will remember my Creator with my whole attention later, when this season ends and the next one is calmer. And the Preacher tells me there is no later that the dark does not eventually swallow. I have been treating my best years as a rehearsal for a remembering I keep filing under next year. Moses prayed against exactly this: "teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12). I have not been numbering them. I have been spending them as though the supply were endless, which is the one thing it is not.

The mercy here is sharp and real. The God the Preacher tells the young to remember is not waiting to catch them in the dark. He is the Creator who gave the light, who scattered the days as a gift, and who came down into the vapor himself, took on a body that would fail, walked toward his own house of mourning on purpose, so that the dust which returns to the earth would not be the end of us. Remember him before the dark, not because he will abandon you in it, but because he went into the dark first to break it open from the inside. The dust returns to the earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it, and the God who gave it is the God who, in Christ, took back his own dust from the grave and carried it up alive. The grave that swallows the Preacher's old man was swallowed itself by a Sunday morning. So sow now. Rejoice now, soberly, under his eye. And remember him now, while it is still day and the doors on the street are still open.

Remember him before the dark.

## The End of the Matter
*When every road under the sun has been walked to its end*

**Text:** Ecclesiastes 12:9-14 · **Supporting:** Matthew 22:37; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Micah 6:8; Romans 2:16

The Preacher has walked every road. Pleasure, work, wisdom, wealth, justice, time, generosity, he has taken each one to the end and come back to report that under the sun they all run out. Now he stops walking. He sits you down, and he gives you the conclusion of a life spent searching, and it is shorter than you expect and weightier than you are ready for.

**The honest teacher**
First he tells you what kind of man you have been listening to. "Besides being wise, the Preacher also taught the people knowledge, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care. The Preacher sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth" (Ecclesiastes 12:9-10). Words of delight and words of truth, both, together, which is the hardest combination in the world to hold. He did not flatter you and he did not crush you. And he tells you what wisdom feels like when it does its job: "The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd" (12:11). Goads. The sharp stick that drives the ox forward when it would rather stand still. Nails that hold and do not let go. This book was never meant to comfort you into sleep. It was meant to prod you awake and fix something in you that you cannot pry loose later.

Then, with the weariness of a man who has read everything, he warns against mistaking the search for the answer: "Of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh" (12:12). He is the wisest reader in Scripture, and he tells you that you will not study your way out of the vapor. The endless library does not contain the conclusion. The conclusion is not long. It is two commands, and they fit in a single breath.

**Fear God. Keep his commandments.**
"The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man" (12:13). After all of it, every test, every road, every disappointment, every dead end under the sun, the whole duty of man fits in two clauses. Fear God. Keep his commandments. Everything under the sun came up vapor; the only thing that does not evaporate is reverence for the One above the sun and a life ordered under his word. This is not a small ending tacked onto a dark book. It is the Preacher closing the ceiling he opened in chapter one, putting God back over the sun, and telling you that this single fact changes the meaning of every road you have walked.

Then the final reason, and it lands like a verdict because it is one: "For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil" (12:14). Every deed. Every secret thing. The Preacher who said the wise and the fool share one grave now tells you the grave is not the end of the account, there is a judgment beyond it, and it reaches the hidden things no one ever saw. Micah compressed the whole law to the same point: "He has told you, O man, what is good... to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8). And Jesus gathered the commandments into love, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind" (Matthew 22:37). The fear of God and the love of God are not rivals. They are the same posture before the same throne.

**The secret things and the cross**
This is where the book stops being theoretical for me, because I have hidden things. Every deed, every secret thing, whether good or evil, the Preacher's last word reaches the room I keep locked, the motives I have never confessed from any pulpit, the parts of me that look one way in the light and another in the dark when no one is watching. I have preached judgment as a doctrine while quietly assuming it would grade me on the public version of my life, the edited one. It will not. Paul says the same with no escape clause: "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:10), and "God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus" (Romans 2:16). The secrets. The Preacher and the apostle agree, and it should terrify any honest man, and it terrifies me, and I think it should.

And here is the only thing that lets a man with secrets walk toward that judgment without despair. The deeds will be brought into judgment, and the One who sits in the judgment seat is the One who already stood in the dock in our place. Every secret thing will be exposed, and the cross is where the exposure already happened, where God brought our hidden evil into judgment and bore the verdict himself instead of handing it to us. The Preacher could only tell you to fear God and keep his commandments, and you have not, and neither have I, not for a single day. The gospel is that the God we are to fear came down under the sun, kept the commandments we broke, and took the judgment for the secret things into his own body on a tree, so that the fear of God and the mercy of God meet for us at one cross. The whole duty of man is still fear God and keep his commandments, that has not changed, and you cannot do it, and neither can I. But the One who commands it also kept it in our place and bore the judgment for the secret things himself. So fear him. The judgment is real, and it reaches the locked room, and it is coming. And he is also, somehow, for you.

Fear God. Keep his commandments.
